nodes.title: Slopsquatting
nodes.short: AI coding assistants sometimes recommend packages that do not exist. Attackers can register those names with malware, an attack called slopsquatting.
nodes.long: Language models that write code sometimes recommend software packages that do not exist. In a study by Spracklen and colleagues (USENIX Security 2025), 16 models produced 576,000 code samples, and about 19.7 percent of the recommended packages were not real, a total of 205,474 invented names. The rate was 21.7 percent for open-source models and 5.2 percent for commercial ones. Many invented names recurred across runs, so an attacker can register a likely name with malware and wait for developers to install it. The term slopsquatting is attributed to Seth Larson of the Python Software Foundation. It adapts typosquatting, in which a malicious package takes a name close to a popular one. The study and the attribution could not be checked at the source, so the figures are as recalled.

nodes.title: Prompt Injection and the Lethal Trifecta
nodes.short: Text hidden in content that an AI agent reads can steer it. An agent with private data, untrusted input and a way to send data out can be made to leak.
nodes.long: Prompt injection is an attack in which text placed in material an AI model reads, such as a web page, an issue or a document, is treated by the model as instructions. In June 2025 Simon Willison named a dangerous combination the lethal trifecta: an agent that can read private data, is exposed to untrusted content and can communicate externally can be steered into leaking data. April 2025 analyses of the Model Context Protocol flagged prompt injection and poisoned tools as ways to exfiltrate data. Mitigations in current practice are limited permissions, sandboxes, allowlists and a separate classifier that blocks scope escalation; Claude Code's documentation warns that after about ten approvals people click through instead of reviewing. It is a close cousin of SQL injection, where attacker text is interpreted as code.
nodes.sleeper: In 1990 a program's code and its input data were kept apart by design. An LLM agent reads both as text, so content it is merely asked to read can end up steering what it does.

nodes.title: AI Slop Vulnerability Reports
nodes.short: In 2025 curl's maintainer reported being flooded with AI-written bug reports that looked real but were not, costing hours of volunteer time per report.
nodes.long: On 14 July 2025 Daniel Stenberg, the lead maintainer of curl, described how AI-generated slop was clogging the project's bug bounty. About 20 percent of 2025 submissions were such reports, and only about 5 percent of those in early July were genuine vulnerabilities. The project receives about two security reports a week, and each report occupies three to four people for 30 minutes to three hours. Since the bounty began in 2019 curl had confirmed 81 real vulnerabilities and paid out more than 90,000 dollars. Stenberg published 21 bogus reports, one titled 'Buffer Overflow in strcpy', and weighed ending cash rewards, better filtering or submission fees: 'We need to reduce the amount of sand in the machine.' A recollection that curl ended the bounty in January 2026 is unverified.

refs.label: Stenberg, Death by a thousand slops

nodes.title: Reflections on Trusting Trust
nodes.short: Ken Thompson's 1984 lecture showed a compiler that inserts a hidden backdoor into the programs it compiles, including itself. The source code can look clean.
nodes.long: In his 1984 Turing Award lecture Ken Thompson described a compiler modified to miscompile the Unix login command so that it also accepts a known password, and to re-insert this trick whenever it compiles the compiler itself. The compiler's source code then looks clean even though the binary is compromised. His conclusion was that you cannot trust code you did not totally create yourself, and that no amount of source-level scrutiny protects you from untrusted code; the problem worsens at lower levels such as the assembler, loader and microcode. Russ Cox wrote in 2019 that we are trusting more code with less justification for doing so. The lecture is the foundation for later concern over build tools and dependencies, and reproducible builds are one response.

nodes.title: COBOL and the 2020 Unemployment Systems
nodes.short: In 2020 several US states said they lacked COBOL programmers to adjust unemployment systems. Whether COBOL itself caused the delays is unproven.
nodes.long: During the COVID-19 surge in unemployment claims in 2020, several US states reported a shortage of skilled COBOL programmers to support their legacy unemployment-benefit systems. Many of those systems had been in the process of conversion to modern languages, and the conversion had been put on hold. The IRS rushed to patch its COBOL-based Individual Master File for CARES Act payments. The news reports that spread the story, such as a CNN article of 8 April 2020 about states needing people who know a half-century-old language, could not be retrieved for checking. Whether COBOL itself, rather than a surge in demand and web front ends, caused the delays was not established, so the claim that COBOL caused the failures is unproven. The episode does show how long COBOL systems stay in service.
nodes.sleeper: COBOL, which you may remember as the language of business data processing, still runs benefit and tax systems, and the 2020 episode made that visible to the public.

nodes.title: Healthcare.gov Launch
nodes.short: The US health insurance marketplace site launched on 1 October 2013 and was nearly unusable for weeks, after changing rules and too little end-to-end testing.
nodes.long: Healthcare.gov, the US federal health-insurance marketplace, launched on schedule on 1 October 2013 but was nearly unusable for weeks. The contract with CGI Federal grew from 93.7 million to 292 million dollars before launch, requirements kept changing until summer 2013, and a McKinsey assessment in March 2013 had warned that the effort was behind and at risk. President Obama said there was no excuse on 21 October 2013. Most problems were fixed by the 23 December enrollment deadline, and a later Health and Human Services inspector general report put the total cost at 1.7 billion dollars. Lessons usually drawn are a fixed date combined with changing scope, no end-to-end testing and diffuse accountability among many contractors. A GAO report and the creation of the US Digital Service in 2014 followed, though that GAO report was not checked.

nodes.title: Equifax Breach
nodes.short: Attackers stole data on 147.9 million Americans from Equifax in 2017 through a web-framework flaw that was disclosed months earlier and left unpatched on one system.
nodes.long: Between May and July 2017 attackers stole personal data on 147.9 million Americans, 15.2 million Britons and about 19,000 Canadians from Equifax. A House Oversight report says a flaw in Apache Struts was publicly disclosed on 7 March 2017 and the Department of Homeland Security alerted Equifax the next day, but an internet-facing dispute portal, a decades-old custom system, was never patched. The attack began on 13 May and ran 76 days; Wikipedia gives 12 May. Attackers ran about 9,000 queries on 48 databases and found unencrypted personal data 265 times. The device that inspected the portal's traffic had been inactive because of an expired certificate, so the theft went unseen until the certificate was renewed on 29 July. The chief executive left on 26 September 2017, and the report cites a lack of accountability and no clear lines of authority in IT management.

refs.label: US House Oversight Committee, Equifax report (2018)

nodes.title: FBI Virtual Case File
nodes.short: The FBI's Virtual Case File was abandoned in April 2005 after about 170 million dollars, because of shifting requirements, rushed schedules and weak oversight.
nodes.long: The Virtual Case File was a case-management system built as part of the Trilogy modernization announced in September 2000. SAIC won a cost-plus contract in mid-2001, and the system was abandoned in April 2005 after about 170 million dollars; IEEE Spectrum called it possibly the most highly publicized software failure in history. The Justice Department Inspector General's 2005 audit, by Glenn Fine, listed eight contributing factors, including poorly defined and slowly evolving design requirements, overly ambitious schedules and no plan to guide hardware purchases. The FBI went through three chief information officers in 2003. The lessons drawn are unstable requirements, cost-plus contracts without technical oversight and schedule pressure after the September 2001 attacks. The 2005 audit itself could not be retrieved, so this rests on secondary reports.

refs.label: IEEE Spectrum: Who Killed the Virtual Case File?

nodes.title: NHS National Programme for IT
nodes.short: The UK programme to create national electronic care records grew from 2.3 to 12.4 billion pounds and was largely dismantled in 2011.
nodes.long: The National Programme for IT in the NHS was set up in October 2002 to give the health service national electronic care records. It was first expected to cost 2.3 billion pounds over three years; by 2006 the National Audit Office put it at 12.4 billion over ten. In 2007 the chair of Parliament's Public Accounts Committee called it the biggest IT project in the world turning into the biggest disaster. In May 2011 the NAO concluded that the 2.7 billion pounds spent so far on care-records systems did not represent value for money and that it had no grounds for confidence about the further 4.3 billion planned. Most of the programme was dismantled in 2011, and the committee later called it among the worst and most expensive contracting fiascos. Lessons drawn are centralized top-down procurement, little involvement of users and clinicians, vendor lock-in and weak contract enforcement.

refs.label: National Audit Office: The National Programme for IT in the NHS, an update (2011)

nodes.title: SOAP and WS-*
nodes.short: SOAP wrapped remote calls in verbose XML and was extended by dozens of vendor-driven WS-* specifications. REST with JSON proved simpler and won.
nodes.long: SOAP was a way for programs to call each other over the network by exchanging XML messages, and large vendors backed it. Version 1.1 was submitted to the W3C as a Note on 8 May 2000 by authors from DevelopMentor, IBM, Microsoft and others, and dozens of vendor-driven add-on specifications, grouped as WS-*, followed. Verbose XML envelopes and that pile of extras lost to REST, the style Roy Fielding described in his 2000 dissertation, combined with JSON, which became an Internet standard, RFC 8259, in December 2017. Michi Henning wrote that SOAP 'had serious technical shortcomings, but, as a market strategy, it was a masterstroke'. No survey figures on how much XML or SOAP remains in use were found, so the decline is inferred from the history of standards.

refs.label: RFC 8259: The JSON Data Interchange Format

nodes.title: XHTML 2.0
nodes.short: The W3C's strict, XML-based XHTML 2 broke compatibility with existing web pages. Its working group lapsed in 2009, and the compatible HTML5 became the standard.
nodes.long: XHTML 2.0 was a W3C effort, running from about 2002, to rebuild HTML as a strict XML language that was not backward compatible with existing pages. The W3C let the working group's charter lapse at the end of 2009. The WHATWG, formed in 2004 by engineers from Apple, Mozilla and Opera, had instead pushed a backward-compatible HTML5, which became a W3C Recommendation in October 2014; since 2019 the WHATWG's living standard has been the single HTML specification. The episode is cited as an example of backward compatibility beating a clean-slate redesign, as AMD's 64-bit x86 did over Itanium. These dates come from secondary sources, and the specific W3C news item was not found.

nodes.title: Removed C++ Features
nodes.short: C++ has dropped or reworked several features that proved too hard to implement or use, including export templates, auto_ptr and exception specifications.
nodes.long: Several C++ features were removed or replaced after they proved too complex. Export templates, ratified in C++98, had only one implementation, from EDG, five years later, and a 2003 proposal to make them optional was defeated by 80 percent; the keyword was dropped for templates in C++11 and reused for modules in C++20. The std::auto_ptr smart pointer, deprecated in C++11 and removed in C++17, was replaced by unique_ptr, and C++17 also removed trigraphs, the register keyword and dynamic exception specifications. Cfront 4.0 was abandoned in 1993 after a failed attempt to add exceptions. Template error messages, which Bjarne Stroustrup called spectacularly long and unhelpful, were improved by concepts in C++20; one test with clang 21.1.0 produced 126 diagnostic lines before concepts and 22 after.

refs.label: Stroustrup, HOPL-III: Evolving a language in and for the real world
